# Incident Report — STRRAT RAT Infection

**Evidence:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 packets, 2024-07-30 06:38:48–06:48:34 UTC, 585.7 sec capture). No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived entirely from packet-level analysis with tshark.

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.16.1.66** |
| MAC address | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** |
| Logged-in user | **ccollier** |
| OS (self-reported) | Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, 64-bit |
| Domain/DC | wiresharkworkshop.online (DC at 172.16.1.4, WIRESHARK-WS-DC) |

Host and user were confirmed via NBNS name registration, Kerberos `CNameString` (ccollier), and directly from the malware's own C2 beacon payload (below), which self-reports hostname and username.

## 2. Malware Family

**STRRAT** (Java-based RAT/RAT-as-a-service).

**Attribution: signature-confirmed.** The infected host opened a plaintext (non-TLS) TCP session to `141.98.10.79:12132` and transmitted a repeating, length-prefixed check-in string that contains the malware's literal name and matches STRRAT's known pipe-delimited ping format verbatim:

```
136\r\n\r\n
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

Field breakdown observed: `ping` marker | family name `STRRAT` | bot/client ID `1BE8292C` | hostname | username | OS | architecture | installed AV (`Windows Defender`) | base64-encoded active window title (`UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` = `Program Manager`) | malware version `1.6` | geolocation `US:United States` | secondary-AV field `Not Installed` | uptime counter incrementing every ~5 seconds (`1 Sec` → `5 min 10 sec`, tcp.stream 83, frames 9066–11562, running continuously to the end of the capture).

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### Command-and-Control
| Type | Value |
|---|---|
| C2 IP:port | **141.98.10.79:12132** (raw TCP, unencrypted, no DNS lookup preceding it — hardcoded IP) |
| Beacon interval | ~5 seconds, plaintext STRRAT ping protocol |
| First beacon | t+76.99s into capture (frame 9066, SYN); STRRAT ping strings begin frame 9119 |
| Client/bot ID | `1BE8292C` |

### Supporting infrastructure (staging/recon, observed via DNS + TLS SNI)
| Domain | Resolved IP | Role |
|---|---|---|
| github.com | 140.82.113.3 | Queried t+63.96s, immediately before C2 contact — likely payload/loader staging (TLS, contents not visible) |
| objects.githubusercontent.com | 185.199.110.133 | Same (largest single non-AD flow after C2, 833 KB over TLS) |
| repo1.maven.org | 199.232.196.209 | Queried t+63.97s–67.97s; largest data transfer in the capture (~4.5 MB over TLS, tcp.stream to 199.232.196.209:443) — consistent with a Java RAT pulling JAR dependencies |
| javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com | 23.194.164.136 | Queried at t+340s — Oracle Java runtime download endpoint, consistent with STRRAT's Java dependency |
| ip-api.com | 208.95.112.1 (via HTTP, port 80) | `GET /json/` at t+77.87s (frame 9111), plaintext, returned public IP geolocation `US/TX/Austin` — used by the malware to populate the `US:United States` field in its beacon, sent one second after C2 registration |

No cleartext file transfer, filename, or hash was recoverable for the GitHub/Maven/Oracle downloads — those sessions are TLS-encrypted end to end (only the TLS ClientHello SNI is visible), so no SHA256 or file name can be grounded in this evidence. No `http` file objects were exported from the capture (`--export-objects http` yielded none beyond the ip-api.com JSON and a benign Microsoft NCSI connectivity check).

### Malicious URL (cleartext, confirmed)
- `http://ip-api.com/json/` (reconnaissance/geolocation lookup, not itself malicious infrastructure but used by the implant)

## 4. Summary Timeline (relative to capture start)
- t=0–65s: Normal AD/Windows domain traffic (Kerberos, LDAP, SMB, DNS to the DC).
- t=63.96s: DNS lookups for github.com and repo1.maven.org — likely payload/dependency staging.
- t=64–68s: ~4.5 MB TLS transfer to repo1.maven.org (199.232.196.209:443) — largest flow in the capture.
- t=76.99s: TCP SYN to 141.98.10.79:12132 — C2 channel established.
- t=78.07s: First STRRAT plaintext ping beacon sent (`STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|...`).
- t=77.87s: Plaintext HTTP GET to ip-api.com/json/ for geolocation.
- t=78s–585s (end of capture): STRRAT beacon repeats every ~5 seconds without interruption; capture ends mid-infection (uptime counter still climbing at "5 min 10 sec").

## 5. Recommended Immediate Actions
- Isolate DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66) from the network.
- Block/monitor 141.98.10.79:12132 at the perimeter.
- Reset credentials for user ccollier (domain account, given AD activity on this session).
- Hunt other hosts for connections to 141.98.10.79:12132 or beacon strings containing `STRRAT|`.
- Acquire host-based forensics (memory, disk) to recover the STRRAT JAR/loader and any dropped files — not visible in this network-only evidence set due to TLS on the delivery channel.
